claims.text: Substituting approximately 2 at.% of a refractory element in equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with Al will improve oxygen resistance.
The Al addition will promote in situ formation of an adherent, slow-growing Al2O3 protective scale.
Approximately 2 at.% Al can be added without significantly degrading room-temperature or high-temperature mechanical properties.
Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr has room-temperature tensile ductility of 8–16%.
Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr has yield strength as high as 530 MPa at 1000 °C.
Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr has inadequate oxygen resistance and undergoes rapid oxidation or pesting during high-temperature air exposure.
The compositional intervention consists of replacing about 2 atomic-percentage points of a refractory element, exemplified by Ti, with Al.
Air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours matches previous oxidation-testing conditions relevant to this alloy.
Mechanical evaluation near 1000 °C at strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1 matches previous testing conditions.
The modified alloy will form a continuous, adherent, and stable Al2O3 surface layer.
Al is more reactive with oxygen than the refractory elements in HfNbTaTiZr and will therefore oxidize preferentially.
The resulting alumina scale has sufficiently low oxygen diffusivity to impede further oxygen ingress.
Reduced oxygen ingress will mitigate bulk oxidation and pesting.
The Al addition and oxide-scale formation will not compromise the underlying microstructure responsible for mechanical properties.
Compared with untreated HfNbTaTiZr, the Al-modified alloy will have a significantly lower oxidation mass gain after 5 hours in air at 800 °C.
Compared with untreated HfNbTaTiZr, the Al-modified alloy will exhibit less oxide-scale spallation after 5 hours in air at 800 °C.
The Al-modified alloy will retain room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength comparable to the untreated alloy.
Oxidation behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys depends strongly on alloy composition and testing conditions.
